title: HE GREW UP SURROUNDED BY CORRUPT PRIESTS… SO WHY DID SAMUEL REFUSE TO WALK AWAY FROM GOD?
paragraphs: HE GREW UP SURROUNDED BY CORRUPT PRIESTS… SO WHY DID SAMUEL REFUSE TO WALK AWAY FROM GOD?
When the people who were supposed to represent God became the reason others despised Him, one young boy made a choice that still confronts every wounded believer today.
What if the greatest threat to your faith isn't the devil attacking you… but the people who taught you to believe in God?
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is struggling to pray, not because they stopped believing in Jesus, but because someone who claimed to represent Him broke their trust.
Someone who preached holiness was living a double life.
Someone who spoke about love became the reason they cried themselves to sleep.
Someone who stood behind a pulpit was hiding things they would never dare confess in front of the congregation.
And now that wounded person is asking a question they never imagined asking.
"If these are God's people… why should I keep serving Him?"
That question is not new.
Thousands of years ago, a young boy named Samuel was growing up in a place where the worship of God was being dishonored by the very men entrusted to protect it.
And what makes his story so extraordinary is not simply that he survived that environment.
It's that Samuel continued ministering before the LORD while corruption was happening around him.
But there is something even more astonishing.
The Bible never tells us Samuel was immune to the darkness around him. It never records every thought he had or every emotion he experienced.
What it does reveal is a young servant whose life was being shaped by God in a place where other men were abusing sacred responsibilities.
And the contrast should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the greatest scandal is not what happens outside the house of God.
Sometimes it is what people have learned to tolerate inside it.
In 1 Samuel 2, we meet Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, the priest who served at the sanctuary in Shiloh.
These were not ordinary men who happened to make occasional mistakes.
They held priestly responsibilities.
They were supposed to help Israel worship the LORD according to His commands.
They should have been examples of reverence, restraint, justice, and obedience.
Instead, Scripture delivers a devastating verdict.
"Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD." — 1 Samuel 2:12, KJV
Consider the original Hebrew.
The expression בְּנֵי בְלִיָּעַל (bene veliyya'al) means, in this context, men characterized by worthlessness or wickedness. The traditional King James rendering is "sons of Belial."
The verse continues with לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת־יְהוָה (lo yad'u et-YHWH) — "they did not know the LORD."
That statement is staggering.
They worked in a sacred environment.
They were connected to a priestly family.
They handled matters associated with worship.
Yet Scripture says they did not know the LORD.
They had religious position without faithful devotion.
They had access to holy things without treating them as holy.
They were close to the sanctuary, but their conduct exposed how far their hearts were from God.
And isn't that one of the most frightening possibilities in Christianity today?
To know the language of faith without knowing the Lord of faith.
To sing about surrender while refusing to surrender.
To teach repentance while secretly defending the very sin we condemn in others.
To appear spiritually alive in public while becoming increasingly hardened in private.
Jesus would later warn about people who honor God with their lips while their hearts remain far from Him (Matthew 15:8).
And that warning reaches beyond priests, pastors, ministry leaders, and public Christian figures.
It reaches you.
It reaches me.
Because before we ask whether someone else has become spiritually compromised, we must be willing to ask whether we have allowed anything in our own hearts to become comfortable with sin.
But the corruption in Shiloh was not merely private hypocrisy.
It was harming other people.
According to 1 Samuel 2:13–17, Eli's sons and their servants were taking portions of sacrificial meat in ways that violated the proper handling of offerings.
They even demanded meat before the fat had been burned, disregarding what belonged to the LORD.
And when worshipers objected, the response could become threatening.
Imagine coming to worship God with a sacrifice, only to encounter men who treated your offering as an opportunity for personal gain.
Imagine bringing something sacred, only to have someone in spiritual authority turn it into an instrument of intimidation.
The text says:
"Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD." — 1 Samuel 2:17, KJV
This is where the story becomes painfully contemporary.
Their sin did not remain contained within their own lives.
It damaged other people's relationship with worship.
Their corruption made the offering of the LORD despised.
And perhaps you understand that kind of damage.
Maybe you once loved going to church.
Maybe you served enthusiastically.
Maybe you gave generously, trusted deeply, and believed the people guiding you would protect what was sacred.
Then something happened.
A betrayal.
An abuse of authority.
A manipulation disguised as spiritual guidance.
A leader who demanded accountability from everyone except himself.
And suddenly the place that once felt safe became a place you could barely enter without remembering what happened.
If that is your story, hear this carefully.
God did not call Eli's sons righteous simply because they held religious office.
He exposed their evil.
He condemned their wrongdoing.
And He did not demand that the people pretend nothing was wrong.
That matters.
Because remaining faithful to God does not mean defending corrupt leaders.
Forgiveness does not require covering up abuse.
Grace does not mean abandoning justice.
And honoring God never requires you to surrender your safety to someone who misuses spiritual authority.
Sometimes faithfulness means speaking the truth, seeking protection, reporting wrongdoing, and refusing to participate in what dishonors the LORD.
Now look at the next verse.
After describing the terrible sins of Eli's sons, Scripture turns our attention to a boy.
"But Samuel ministered before the LORD, being a child, girded with a linen ephod." — 1 Samuel 2:18, KJV
Two words deserve your attention.
But Samuel.
While corruption was spreading…
But Samuel.
While sacred offerings were being dishonored…
But Samuel.
While men with religious authority were acting without reverence…
But Samuel.
The Hebrew begins:
וּשְׁמוּאֵל מְשָׁרֵת אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה
U-Shemu'el mesharet et-penei YHWH.
A close rendering is, "And Samuel was ministering before the LORD."
The verb מְשָׁרֵת (mesharet) describes Samuel as one serving or ministering.
Notice where Scripture places the focus.
Not on Samuel serving the reputation of Eli's family.
Not on Samuel protecting the image of the sanctuary.
Not on Samuel seeking approval from Hophni and Phinehas.
Samuel was ministering before the LORD.
That distinction changes everything.
He was not serving because the people around him were perfect.
He was serving before the God who remained holy despite their corruption.
And that is where some of us have lost our spiritual footing.
We attached our faith so tightly to a person that when the person fell, we felt as though God had fallen with them.
We confused the messenger with the Savior.
We confused the institution with the Kingdom.
We confused a leader's character with God's character.
And when the leader failed, our trust in God began to collapse.
But Samuel's story invites us to make a distinction that can save our faith from being swallowed by someone else's sin.
The failure of a person who claims to represent God is not the failure of God Himself.
The sins of Eli's sons were real.
The damage they caused was real.
God's judgment against them was real.
But their wickedness did not make the LORD wicked.
Their unfaithfulness did not make Him unfaithful.
Their abuse of sacred things did not make Him less holy.
And their position did not give them ownership over the God they claimed to serve.
Perhaps that is something your wounded heart needs to hear tonight.
The person who hurt you does not get to define Jesus for you.
The person who betrayed you does not get the final word over your relationship with God.
And the scandal you witnessed does not have to become the final chapter of your faith.
But there is another detail in Samuel's story that makes it even more beautiful.
He did not arrive at Shiloh by accident.
His mother, Hannah, had once endured deep sorrow because she could not have a child.
She prayed to the LORD in anguish.
She was misunderstood even while she was pouring out her heart before God.
And when God answered her prayer, she fulfilled her vow by bringing Samuel to serve at the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1:11, 24–28).
Think about the weight of that.
Hannah entrusted her beloved son to the LORD.
Yet the environment where Samuel would grow up included deeply corrupt priests.
The text does not tell us Hannah knew beforehand everything that was happening among Eli's sons.
Nor does it tell us she approved of their behavior.
What it shows is that the LORD's purposes for Samuel were not defeated by the wickedness of those men.
Hannah had prayed for a son.
God had heard her.
And now that son was growing in service before Him.
"And the child Samuel grew on, and was in favour both with the LORD, and also with men." — 1 Samuel 2:26, KJV
While Hophni and Phinehas were moving toward judgment, Samuel was growing.
While their conduct was bringing dishonor, Samuel's life was developing in a different direction.
Same sanctuary.
Same religious environment.
Different response to God.
And that should challenge the way we think about our own lives.
Your environment influences you, but it does not have to determine your final allegiance.
The sins you witnessed do not have to become the sins you imitate.
The hypocrisy that wounded you does not have to become the hypocrisy you practice.
By God's grace, a different path remains possible.
But do not misunderstand this.
Samuel's example is not a command for victims to remain in dangerous religious environments.
His story describes God's work in his particular circumstances. It does not establish a universal rule that faithful believers must endure abuse or remain under corrupt leadership.
The deeper lesson is that even when human representatives fail, the LORD remains worthy of our trust and obedience.
And then the story becomes darker.
Eli was not ignorant of his sons' behavior.
According to 1 Samuel 2:22–25, he heard about their wrongdoing, including their sexual misconduct involving women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
He rebuked them.
But they would not listen.
Later, the LORD's message against Eli's household revealed the seriousness of his failure to restrain them.
In 1 Samuel 3:13, God declared that Eli knew about his sons' iniquity and had not adequately restrained them.
This is not merely a warning against committing evil.
It is a warning about knowing evil is taking place and failing to exercise the responsibility God has entrusted to us.
And that warning should trouble every spiritual leader.
Because there are moments when silence is not wisdom.
There are moments when protecting an organization's reputation becomes a way of abandoning the people who were harmed.
There are moments when preserving a ministry's appearance becomes more important to its leaders than repentance, truth, and justice.
And Scripture does not treat that as harmless.
God held Eli's household accountable.
The LORD sent a man of God to announce judgment in 1 Samuel 2:27–36.
Then, in chapter 3, the judgment was confirmed through a message delivered to Samuel.
God was not indifferent.
He had seen.
He had heard.
He would judge.
And if you have ever wondered whether God notices what people do behind religious appearances, the story of Shiloh gives a sobering answer.
God sees what religious reputation can conceal.
Yet here is the moment that makes Samuel's story unforgettable.
1 Samuel 3 opens with a chilling description of the spiritual atmosphere.
"And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision." — 1 Samuel 3:1, KJV
The word translated "precious" comes from the Hebrew יָקָר (yaqar), which in this context carries the sense of being rare.
Revelatory words from the LORD were uncommon.
The text does not mean God had ceased to exist, stopped caring, or lost His power.
It means that prophetic revelation was not frequently being received.
And in that setting, a young Samuel lay down for the night.
Eli's eyesight had grown dim.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out.
Samuel was lying down in the sanctuary area, near where the ark of God was located.
Then something happened.
A voice called his name.
"Samuel."
He answered, "Here am I."
Thinking Eli had called him, Samuel ran to the elderly priest.
But Eli said he had not called.
Samuel returned and lay down.
Then the voice came again.
"Samuel."
Again he went to Eli.
Again Eli told him to return.
A third time the LORD called.
And finally Eli understood what was happening.
The LORD was calling the boy.
He instructed Samuel how to respond.
Then came the moment.
"And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth." — 1 Samuel 3:10, KJV
Imagine the stillness.
The sanctuary was quiet.
The young servant was listening.
And the God whose worship had been dishonored by corrupt priests was now speaking to Samuel.
But we must be careful not to romanticize what happened next.
God did not simply give Samuel a comforting message about his future.
He entrusted him with a terrifying announcement.
Judgment was coming upon Eli's household.
The message was so serious that Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision (1 Samuel 3:15).
And here we discover another dimension of faithfulness.
Serving God is not always emotionally comfortable.
Sometimes obedience requires hearing truths we wish were not true.
Sometimes it means speaking with courage when silence would feel safer.
Sometimes it means refusing to conceal wrongdoing, even when the people involved have been important figures in our lives.
Eli pressed Samuel to tell him what the LORD had said.
And Samuel told him everything.
He did not hide the message.
"And Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing from him." — 1 Samuel 3:18, KJV
There it is.
A young servant, growing up in a spiritually compromised environment, was willing to speak the truth of God.
Not because he was stronger than everyone else.
Not because Scripture portrays him as incapable of fear.
The text explicitly says he was afraid.
But he still delivered the message.
And perhaps that is what courage really looks like.
Not the absence of trembling.
But obedience even while trembling.
Maybe you have been afraid to tell the truth.
Afraid to confront something you know is wrong.
Afraid that acknowledging what happened will disappoint people you love.
Afraid that exposing wrongdoing will make others accuse you of attacking the Church.
But the Church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And Christ does not need lies to defend His name.
Truthful accountability is not the enemy of genuine faith.
Unrepentant sin is.
Now here is where we must look beyond Samuel.
Because if this story ends with "Be like Samuel," we will have missed the greatest hope Scripture offers.
Samuel was a faithful servant whom God raised up.
But Samuel was not the Savior.
He was not sinless.
He was not the final answer to Israel's need.
And even his story reminds us that human leadership remains imperfect. Later, 1 Samuel 8:1–3 records that Samuel's own sons did not walk in his ways.
That detail is humbling.
No human family can guarantee faithfulness from one generation to the next.
No religious office can manufacture a transformed heart.
No human leader can carry the weight of being our ultimate hope.
And that is why the story must ultimately lead us to Jesus Christ.
Where corrupt priests dishonored holy things, Jesus is our holy and faithful High Priest.
Where sinful human leaders used religious responsibility for their own benefit, Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
Where earthly priests failed, Jesus remains the One who perfectly fulfills His priestly work.
Hebrews 7:26 describes Him as:
"For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens." — KJV
The Greek word ἀμίαντος (amiantos) means undefiled or unstained.
Jesus is not merely a better religious leader.
He is the sinless Son of God.
He did not come to exploit wounded people.
He came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10).
He did not come to enrich Himself through the suffering of sinners.
He gave His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
And when religious authorities rejected Him, when false accusations surrounded Him, when human injustice reached its terrible climax at the cross, Jesus did not abandon the Father's saving purpose.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
This is the Gospel.
Not that good people can somehow remain good enough to survive a corrupt world.
But that sinners can be forgiven and made new through the crucified and risen Christ.
This is why we keep coming back to Him.
Not because every church leader is trustworthy.
Not because every Christian community is healthy.
Not because our experiences have always been beautiful.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy even when those who speak His name are not acting faithfully.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you are not Hophni or Phinehas.
Maybe you have not abused a position of spiritual authority.
But perhaps there are sins you have been excusing because no one has discovered them.
Perhaps your public Christianity looks stronger than your private obedience.
Perhaps you are angry at hypocrisy in others while quietly tolerating compromise in yourself.
If so, the answer is not to hide more carefully.
It is to repent.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin and toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed after being exposed.
It is not merely regretting the consequences.
It is coming honestly before God, acknowledging our sin, and turning toward Him in faith and obedience.
And the astonishing news is that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not erase earthly consequences or remove the need to make wrongs right.
But it does mean that the grace of God is greater than the shame that tells you to remain hidden.
Maybe you are the person who has been wounded.
Then your next step may not look like someone else's.
You may need time to grieve.
You may need trustworthy support.
You may need to leave an unsafe environment.
You may need to report misconduct and seek appropriate help.
And you may need to rediscover the character of Jesus apart from the behavior of someone who misrepresented Him.
You do not have to pretend the wound was small.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to trust an unrepentant person simply because they use Christian language.
But you can bring your pain to Christ.
He knows what betrayal is.
He knows what false accusation is.
He knows what it means to be abandoned.
And because He is risen, the darkness that wounded you does not have authority to determine your eternity.
That is the hope of redemption.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
But discovering that the grace of Jesus Christ can write a future the scandal could never produce.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps tonight, your prayer is not eloquent.
Perhaps all you can say is:
"Lord, I still believe in You, but I am struggling to trust people."
Or:
"Jesus, I have been pretending to be stronger than I really am."
Or:
"Father, I have spent so much time condemning other people's sins that I have stopped confronting my own."
Or perhaps:
"Lord, I want to come back. I just don't know where to begin."
Start there.
With honesty.
With repentance where repentance is needed.
With the willingness to listen to God's Word.
And with your eyes fixed on Jesus, not on the perfection of human beings.
Samuel did not have to become like Eli's sons simply because he lived near them.
And you do not have to become spiritually cynical simply because you have witnessed religious hypocrisy.
You can reject corruption without rejecting Christ.
You can seek justice without surrendering to bitterness.
You can acknowledge your wounds without making them your identity.
You can begin again.
Not because your willpower is unlimited.
But because God's grace is real.
And if you have reached this point, I want to ask you something deeply personal.
What has been harder for you: continuing to believe in God after being hurt by people, or forgiving yourself for the ways you have failed Him?
You do not need to tell the whole story publicly. Protect your privacy, especially when abuse or trauma is involved.
Your words may become the reminder someone else needs: they are not the only one struggling to remain faithful.
And if this message brought someone to mind, please do not let it end with you.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have become spiritually complacent, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
Because the goal is not simply to build a large audience.
The goal is to keep pointing people to the Savior.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Christ, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Every article takes time to prepare. Every Scripture must be handled carefully. Every message should point beyond the writer to Jesus Christ.
It can be an expression of generous Christian giving, but it is not a required tithe, a payment for God's favor, or a measure of your faithfulness.
Scripture teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
God-honoring generosity is not supposed to be extracted through guilt.
It grows from a willing heart.
These items can serve as reminders of Scripture, thoughtful gifts, and tools for encouraging conversations about faith.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, not something reserved only for those who can pay.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite others to read it.
Encourage someone to open the Bible.
Help a wounded believer remember that Jesus is not the same as the person who betrayed them.
It would be another person turning back to Christ.
Another hidden sin brought into the light.
Another wounded believer finding courage to pray again.
Another heart discovering that the Gospel is not the story of flawless religious people.
It is the story of a flawless Savior who came to redeem sinners.
A boy was lying down.
A priestly household was under judgment.
The spiritual atmosphere was dark.
And the LORD called:
"Samuel, Samuel."
Samuel answered:
"Speak; for thy servant heareth."
What a remarkable contrast.
Men with sacred positions had refused to listen to God.
Yet a young servant was learning to hear His voice.
And that is the question this ancient story leaves with us.
Not simply, "Why did Samuel continue serving God?"
But:
When the failures of others have wounded your faith, will you still be willing to listen to the One who has never failed you?
You may have been betrayed by someone who carried a Bible.
You may have been disappointed by someone who preached the truth.
You may have seen things in the house of God that should never have happened there.
But do not allow the people who dishonored His name to persuade you that Jesus is unworthy of your trust.
Come back to His Word.
Come back to honest prayer.
Come back to repentance and grace.
Come back to the cross, where the sinless Savior gave His life for the guilty.
Come back to the empty tomb, where death itself could not hold Him.
Because the hope of your salvation was never resting on Eli's sons.
It was never resting on Samuel.
And it was never resting on the religious leader who disappointed you.
Your hope rests in Jesus Christ.
The hands that wounded your faith may have belonged to people who spoke for God, but the nail-scarred hands that can redeem your story belong to Jesus.
